title: The One With All The Kissing

jokes.text: You look cute in bubbles. / You're just all liquored up.
jokes.setup: Monica gives a sweet, sincere compliment about Chandler looking cute in bubbles (presumably a bubble bath)
jokes.punchline: Chandler dismisses the compliment entirely, attributing it to Monica being drunk rather than accepting any affection — classic Chandler deflection
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler self-deprecation and deflection of affection — very much in character, economical, and gets the episode off on the right comedic foot. Functional rather than exceptional; the joke type is very well-worn for this character.

dialogue.speaker: Character A
dialogue.line: You look really cute in bubbles.

dialogue.speaker: Character B
dialogue.line: That's just the alcohol talking.

jokes.text: I've had a very long, hard day. Want some chicken? No, thanks. No chicken. Bye-bye.
jokes.setup: Monica has clearly had an intimate evening and wants privacy; Joey obliviously barges in with an offer of chicken
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of her exhausted romantic state with Joey's mundane chicken offer, plus the childlike 'Bye-bye' dismissal
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey obliviousness landing against Monica's frantic privacy. The 'Bye-bye' is a funny little touch. Functional setup-punchline that plays off character archetypes well.

dialogue.speaker: Character A
dialogue.line: I've had such a difficult day.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Do you want some chicken?

jokes.text: Some extra-crispy, dirty rice? / For the last time, no! Get out, Joey!
jokes.setup: Joey was already told no to chicken; he escalates the offer with increasingly specific side dishes
jokes.punchline: 'For the last time, no!' reveals this has been a prolonged back-and-forth, escalating the absurdity of the standoff
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the chicken bit is pure Joey. 'Extra-crispy, dirty rice' is a lovingly specific food detail that only Joey would use as a persuasion tactic. The escalation earns a bigger laugh than the initial setup.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, how about dinner? I know this great place, they do extra-crispy, dirty rice...

dialogue.speaker: Character A
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But you don't even know what I was gonna—

dialogue.speaker: Character A
dialogue.line: No!

jokes.text: After Chandler complains Joey kept asking if he wanted chicken, Joey immediately pipes up: 'I could eat some chicken.'
jokes.setup: Chandler explains his frustration that Joey 'kept asking me if I wanted chicken' — framing it as an absurd annoyance
jokes.punchline: Joey, having no self-awareness, immediately says 'I could eat some chicken' — proving the entire point in real time
jokes.explanation: A beautifully tight callback that lands because it's perfectly timed: the audience has just heard the complaint and then immediately the complaint proves itself true. Joey's one-track food mind is illustrated with maximum economy (four words). The structure is nearly perfect — setup/complaint/instant ironic demonstration. High character integration; this is pure Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I've got chicken!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No thanks, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's really good chicken.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I said no.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Free chicken.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How much chicken are we talking about?

jokes.text: Joey immediately orders a full chicken meal ('three-piece, some coleslaw, some beans and a Coke') in the middle of the conversation
jokes.setup: 'I could eat some chicken' — Joey has just admitted he wants chicken
jokes.punchline: He immediately places a detailed, specific fast-food order as if he's at a drive-through, mid-scene
jokes.explanation: Extends the chicken gag with a third beat — Joey is so committed to food that he orders mid-scene. The specificity of 'three-piece, coleslaw, beans and a Coke' is funny but it's the third iteration of the same joke, so diminishing returns apply.

dialogue.speaker: Character A
dialogue.line: I'll have a triple cheeseburger, extra bacon, large fries, onion rings, and a fried chicken sandwich.

dialogue.speaker: Character B
dialogue.line: And to drink?

dialogue.speaker: Character A
dialogue.line: Diet Coke.

jokes.text: Diet Coke.
jokes.setup: Joey has just ordered a full chicken meal including a Coke
jokes.punchline: Monica, without missing a beat, amends his order to 'Diet Coke' — both participating in the absurdity and revealing her controlling nature
jokes.explanation: Two words that do enormous work. Monica's controlling personality, her participation in the absurd scene, and the callback to Joey's order all land simultaneously. The economy is essentially perfect — no word could be removed. It's a tag joke that elevates the whole sequence. Only Monica could deliver this line, and it perfectly caps a three-beat running gag. Genuinely exceptional for its brevity.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So there was this cabdriver, right? And he told me...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, weren't you just in London?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, yes! Remember when we went to London?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you didn't go to London.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I went in my mind! Anyway, the cabdriver...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What was London like?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Amazing! So wet. So... British.

jokes.text: Was his name Angus? / What? / He was a cabdriver we had in London.
jokes.setup: Phoebe begins telling a story about a cabdriver; Monica interrupts with a very specific guess at the driver's name
jokes.punchline: The name 'Angus' is absurdly specific and confidently wrong; the reveal that it's a London callback makes it both funnier and more annoying to Phoebe
jokes.explanation: Establishes the episode's secondary comedic thread — the London crew constantly derailing conversations with London nostalgia, excluding Phoebe. Functional, sets up better jokes to come.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Remember when we all went to London for my wedding?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, yes! And remember when Ross got off the plane?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How could we forget? He was only gone for like five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I remember the fish and chips were amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I remember the cobblestone streets. Very spiritual energy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually, I remember every single detail. The way the light hit Big Ben at exactly 3:47 PM.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You remember that specifically?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I remember what everyone was wearing. Rachel had on her blue top with the—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, that's creepy, Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I remember the exact number of steps to the Tower of London. Two thousand, three hundred and forty-seven.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I remember the name of the waiter at that one restaurant. His name was Herbert.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I remember I saw a pigeon that looked exactly like my grandmother. It was a sign.

jokes.text: Phoebe, after being completely shut out of her own story, mutters 'So, he had a really funny hat. I don't want to talk about it.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been completely unable to tell her story due to everyone's London nostalgia hijacking the conversation
jokes.punchline: She delivers a defeated one-line summary of her story — 'he had a really funny hat' — and then gives up entirely
jokes.explanation: The deflation is the joke — the entire buildup of Phoebe trying to tell a story ends with 'he had a really funny hat,' suggesting the story was never interesting to begin with. The 'I don't want to talk about it' caps it with a sulky dignity that is very Phoebe. Well-structured payoff to the previous beat.

dialogue.speaker: Character A
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. Go back to your story. What happened with the guy?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh. Um, nothing. He just... left. That was it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm gonna go get some gum.

jokes.text: Ross walks in, Monica and Chandler yell 'Boddington's!' and he immediately echoes it with equal excitement: 'Oh, man! I'd walk back to London for another frosty one of those bad boys.'
jokes.setup: The London nostalgia running gag continues as Ross enters
jokes.punchline: He not only matches their enthusiasm immediately but escalates with 'I'd walk back to London' — a hyperbolic testament to how good the beer was
jokes.explanation: Extends the London-nostalgia running gag. Ross's hyperbolic enthusiasm ('walk back to London') is mildly funny but this beat is the weakest of the London trio — it's just more of the same with a hyperbole added.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm going to London!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's great! You'll love it there.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Love it? I'm going to have the best beer of my entire life! British ale, mate. It's going to change everything!

jokes.text: Someone mentions they have Boddington's at 'the British pub by the Trade Center,' and everyone immediately abandons the conversation: 'Later!'
jokes.setup: Ross says he'd walk back to London for Boddington's beer
jokes.punchline: Someone reveals there's a pub nearby that has it; everyone drops the conversation and bolts instantly
jokes.explanation: A clean button on the London/Boddington's running gag. The abrupt 'Later!' works because of its economy and the commitment to the bit. Functional cap to the sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I would walk all the way to London for a beer right now.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Couldn't you just go to the store?

jokes.text: Ross says 'Rachel is my wife' — then corrects himself — 'Emily! Emily is my wife.'
jokes.setup: Ross is defending his decision to chase Emily over abandoning Rachel; he's trying to explain Emily is his wife and that takes priority
jokes.punchline: He accidentally says 'Rachel is my wife' — a Freudian slip that reveals his true feelings — and then corrects it flustered
jokes.explanation: A Freudian slip that does double duty — it's funny in the moment and it also carries the season's central dramatic irony. The audience knows Ross's feelings for Rachel are unresolved; this slip confirms it while he's actively trying to claim the opposite. Strong character integration because it only makes sense for Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She's not my wife!

dialogue.speaker: Character A
dialogue.line: Yet.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? No, I mean... she's not... we're not...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I meant to say my girlfriend. Rachel is my girlfriend.

jokes.text: Joey mocking Ross: 'I can't believe she can outrun you.' Ross getting defensive: 'Hey! She's fast, okay? You think you can beat me? Let's go! Outside!'
jokes.setup: Ross explains he lost Emily at the airport because he couldn't catch her
jokes.punchline: Joey's light jab at Ross's athletic ability triggers a hilariously outsized defensive challenge from Ross to race Joey outside
jokes.explanation: Ross's fragile masculinity being punctured by Joey is a reliable well. The escalation to 'Let's go! Outside!' is funny because it's completely disproportionate to the moment. Good character work for both Ross (defensive, nerdy) and Joey (casually devastating).

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? I can run fast! I'll race you right now!

dialogue.speaker: Character A
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah! I'm very athletic. I'll beat you to the door!

jokes.text: Rachel's response to being abandoned in Greece: 'Terrible? Hell, I was in Greece! There was a nice hotel, nice beach, met nice people.'
jokes.setup: Ross apologizes profusely, expecting Rachel to be devastated and furious about being left alone in Greece
jokes.punchline: Rachel completely defuses the expected emotional confrontation by revealing she actually had a great time, entirely undercutting Ross's guilt
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the whole episode's setup was building to Rachel being furious, so the reversal works well structurally. It also sets up the later reveal (her actual feelings) which makes this a double-layered joke in hindsight.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, it was amazing! The beaches were so beautiful, the food was incredible, and the people were so friendly. I had the best time!

jokes.text: Ross reacts to Rachel's good time in Greece with a muttered 'It's not too shabby for Rachel' — talking to himself with a tone of mild, baffled resentment
jokes.setup: Rachel has just said her abandoned-in-Greece experience was actually great
jokes.punchline: Ross, who was expecting forgiveness to be hard-won, mutters to himself as if mildly put out that she had a good time
jokes.explanation: A quiet character beat — Ross's self-centeredness peeking through as he processes that his guilt trip wasn't needed. Functional but not a big laugh — more of a character moment that studio audiences will recognize and chuckle at.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Twelve dozen roses. That's 144 roses. One for each day since we met. Well, actually, I rounded down.

jokes.text: Ross explains he's sending 72 long-stemmed red roses to Emily's parents' house — 'One for each day I've known and loved her.'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying desperately to find Emily after losing her at the airport
jokes.punchline: He's counted exactly how many days he's known her and is sending that exact number of roses — revealing an obsessive, calculating romantic gesture that is both touching and deeply unhinged
jokes.explanation: 72 roses is the kind of specific detail that elevates a joke. It tells us Ross has literally counted the days, which is both romantic and obsessive in a way that is completely true to his character. Sets up a great callback later (the mulched roses).

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? Just say her name right this time.

jokes.text: Phoebe's advice about the card: 'When you make out the card, be sure to make it out to Emily.'
jokes.setup: Ross says the 72 roses 'should get her talking'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe deadpans that he should make sure to write 'Emily' on the card — a callback to his Freudian slip earlier about Rachel being his wife
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's callback to the Freudian slip is delivered with perfect deadpan simplicity. The economy is excellent — she doesn't explain or wink at the audience, she just says it. The rewatch bonus comes from understanding exactly why she says this. Strong structural callback work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It was a nightmare! The hotel was falling apart, the food gave me food poisoning, and I got lost for three days!

dialogue.speaker: Greek Man
dialogue.line: Mrs. Green, you okay?

dialogue.speaker: Another Greek
dialogue.line: Mrs. Green, we find you now, is good!

jokes.text: Rachel's mask drops — she reveals she actually had a terrible time: 'I didn't have a good time in Greece! Ross abandoned me! I couldn't get a plane out!'
jokes.setup: Rachel has just told Ross she had a great time and 'we're totally cool' — the moment Ross leaves, Phoebe comments on how great it was
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately breaks down, revealing everything she said was a front: she was humiliated, stuck in the hotel suite, had Greeks coming up to her saying 'Mrs. Geller! Why are you cry?'
jokes.explanation: The reveal works as a structural reversal of the earlier misdirection joke. The comedic highlight is the specific detail of Greeks approaching her saying 'Why are you cry?' — the broken English and the humiliation of being known as 'Mrs. Geller' is funny and painful simultaneously. Good dramatic irony turned into comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I've made so many bad decisions. I'm a mess. My life is a disaster.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Columbus sucks! Columbus sucks! Columbus sucks!

jokes.text: 'People came up to me going, "Mrs. Geller! Why are you cry?"'
jokes.setup: Rachel is describing how humiliated she was being left in Greece as Ross's apparent discarded companion
jokes.punchline: The specific detail of hotel staff approaching her with broken-English concern ('Why are you cry?') is both funny and poignant — the grammatical error makes the moment absurd
jokes.explanation: The broken English 'Why are you cry?' is a memorable specific detail that elevates what could have been a generic complaint. It's specific enough to feel real and the grammatical error adds an inadvertent comic absurdity. High quotability because of the distinctive phrasing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, will you make all my decisions for me?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No. No, I can't do that.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Because I'm not a good person.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'London is stupid! Stupid!'
jokes.setup: Rachel is spiraling about all her bad decisions, blaming herself for going to London for Ross's wedding
jokes.punchline: She escalates to a childlike, petulant declaration that the entire city of London is 'stupid! Stupid!' — an absurdly reductive verdict
jokes.explanation: The childlike regression is funny because Rachel is usually the composed one of the group. 'Stupid! Stupid!' is a funny bit of petulance. Not particularly sophisticated but lands in the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't make your decisions for you, Rachel. I have too much baggage from my past.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'll do it! I'll make all your decisions!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, that's really sweet, but—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, I'm thinking about this. We need to set up a system. Color-coded binders, daily check-ins, I'll need access to your closet for pre-approval of outfits.

jokes.text: Rachel tells Phoebe to make all her decisions; Phoebe says 'Oh no. I did that for someone once. I'm not comfortable having that power over someone's life.'
jokes.setup: Rachel, fed up with her own bad decisions, asks Phoebe to make all her life decisions
jokes.punchline: Phoebe — who is not known for sound judgment — solemnly declines, citing a past experience and her discomfort with having that 'power over someone's life,' implying a dramatic backstory we'll never hear
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Phoebe, of all people, is the one who refuses on the grounds of a traumatic past experience with this responsibility — she speaks with a gravity that implies a whole dark backstory. The character integration is excellent; this is exactly the kind of mysterious past-life hint Phoebe tends to drop.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, please be careful with those! They're originals!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know, I know. I'm being gentle.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Gentle?! You're crying on them! Your tears are literally falling on my memories!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's just a little moisture—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A little moisture?! Do you know what moisture does to photographs from the '80s?!

jokes.text: Monica tells Rachel there are great guys everywhere and suggests Gunther as an example
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to get Rachel to move on from Ross by pointing out eligible men at the coffee shop
jokes.punchline: She points to Gunther — who the audience knows is hopelessly, one-sidedly in love with Rachel — as an example of a 'great guy' who's 'nice' and 'cute'
jokes.explanation: Lands primarily on audience knowledge of the Gunther/Rachel dynamic. Monica is oblivious to Gunther's obsession while simultaneously being right that he's available. The rewatch bonus comes from the dramatic irony of this situation. Functional recurring joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's okay. I know you're going through a lot right now.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Though I'm guessing at least some of that was about me.

jokes.text: Monica tells Rachel about a guy at the counter: 'That's the guy you flirted with at the counter.' Monica makes the decision: 'You'll too talk to him. I make your decisions, and I say you'll too talk to him.'
jokes.setup: Monica has taken on the role of Rachel's decision-maker and is now wielding that authority
jokes.punchline: Monica's controlling nature is fully unleashed — she speaks with absolute authority ('I make your decisions') in a tone that's part best-friend, part dictator
jokes.explanation: Monica's controlling nature finding an outlet here is good character comedy. 'I make your decisions' said with full conviction is funny because of how much she's visibly enjoying this power. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, okay. There's plenty of great guys out there. Like Gunther!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Gunther?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah! He's sweet, he's sensitive, he makes a mean cappuccino...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, Gunther is in love with me. It's weird.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Exactly! He's available!

jokes.text: Rachel: 'You're the boss. I got to do what you tell me.' Monica: 'Say that to him, and you're golden.'
jokes.setup: Rachel submissively agrees to do what Monica says as a romantic approach strategy
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately co-opts Rachel's submission line as a pick-up line, telling Rachel to use 'You're the boss, I do what you tell me' on the guy
jokes.explanation: Clean double meaning — what Rachel says about Monica's authority gets immediately recycled as a flirtatious line. Good economy and Monica's confidence in her own advice is funny. Competent writing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I have to do what you tell me.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, go up to him and say, 'Hi, I'm Rachel, and I have to do whatever you tell me to do.'

jokes.text: We've been talking about London too much. / Sorry, it's just because I couldn't be there. All I get to do now is pregnant stuff. It bums me out.
jokes.setup: Phoebe explains why she's sensitive about London — she was pregnant and couldn't attend
jokes.punchline: The blunt resignation of 'All I get to do now is pregnant stuff. It bums me out.' — describing pregnancy as a bummer with flat, funny understatement
jokes.explanation: 'Pregnant stuff. It bums me out.' is a nicely deflating way to describe carrying triplets as a surrogate. Phoebe's flat delivery of existential inconvenience is a good character note.

jokes.text: Phoebe explains she has a date: 'A little of this, a little of that. I got myself a date tomorrow.' Monica: 'See? Didn't I tell you? You're getting over Ross already.'
jokes.setup: Monica has been coaching Rachel on getting over Ross; she asks what happened with the guy Rachel talked to
jokes.punchline: It turns out it was PHOEBE who got the date, not Rachel — Monica's authority as Rachel's decision-maker is immediately undercut
jokes.explanation: Good beat — Monica's confident praise of Rachel's progress ('You're getting over Ross already!') is immediately undercut by the reveal that it was Phoebe who scored the date. Monica's oblivious confidence makes the reversal funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm pregnant stuff.

jokes.text: After Chandler kisses Monica goodbye on the lips, Joey asks 'What the hell was that?' and Chandler explains: 'Probably some European goodbye thing he picked up in London.'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are secret; Chandler has just kissed Monica on the lips as a goodbye — to everyone's confusion
jokes.punchline: Chandler covers by claiming it's a 'European goodbye thing he picked up in London' — a ridiculous explanation that Joey somewhat buys
jokes.explanation: One of the central comedic engines of Season 5 — Chandler and Monica's secret relationship generating increasingly absurd cover stories. The 'European goodbye thing' cover is funny because it's barely plausible but Chandler commits to it. Rewatch bonus because viewers know the secret.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, why did Joey kiss you goodbye?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's a European thing. He picked it up in... I don't know, Europe.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That felt French.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: His kiss. It felt French.

jokes.text: Rachel stops mid-date to run inside and ask Monica whether she should invite the guy in — Monica is doing laundry
jokes.setup: Rachel is on a date at the door and must decide whether to invite him in; she has assigned Monica decision-making authority over her love life
jokes.punchline: She literally interrupts her own date to run inside to ask Monica — taking the bit to a logical but absurd extreme
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the 'Monica makes Rachel's decisions' setup. The physical comedy of actually running inside mid-date to ask is funny. The joke is in taking the premise literally to its absurd conclusion.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross! You sent Emily flowers?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, I wanted to make a grand romantic gesture.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How'd that work out?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Emily destroyed them and sent them back as mulch.

jokes.text: Ross reveals Emily sent back his 72 roses — 'cut up into mulch.' Monica's response: 'It's not so bad. Monica's going to make potpourri.'
jokes.setup: Ross's grand romantic gesture of 72 roses was returned — shredded into mulch by an enraged Emily
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately finds the silver lining: she's going to make potpourri from the destroyed roses — practical, cheerful, and completely tone-deaf to Ross's heartbreak
jokes.explanation: The callback to the 72 roses pays off brilliantly — Emily's fury expressed through mulching the roses is a great visual, and Monica's pragmatic potpourri response is perfectly in character (she's already making use of it). The dark humor of the mulched romantic gesture is excellent, and 'Monica's going to make potpourri' is a great topper.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, we could make potpourri out of them!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Potpourri? Monica, they were beautiful roses!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: They still are... just in a more... fragrant way.

jokes.text: Ross: 'I think I'm going to go wander out in the rain for a while.' Joey: 'It's not raining.' Ross: 'I can't catch a break!'
jokes.setup: Ross is devastated by the returned mulched roses and wants to do something dramatically sad
jokes.punchline: He announces he'll 'wander out in the rain' for a while — only to be flatly informed by Joey that it's not raining. Ross's subsequent 'I can't catch a break!' applies to both the rain and his life generally
jokes.explanation: A three-beat joke with excellent structure. The setup (dramatic rain wandering), the deflation (it's not raining), and the universalizing punchline ('I can't catch a break!') all click together. 'I can't catch a break' works on multiple levels simultaneously and is quotable. Joey's flat delivery of 'It's not raining' is perfect straight-man work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm going to go wander dramatically in the rain.

dialogue.speaker: Character A
dialogue.line: It's not raining.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, even the weather won't cooperate with my misery!

jokes.text: Monica cancels Rachel's date ('Hey, Dave. I need to take a rain check. My roommate is really sick.') while Rachel is right there
jokes.setup: Ross is upset about the mulched roses and Monica has committed to staying with him; Rachel has a date coming over
jokes.punchline: Monica exercises her decision-making power by canceling Rachel's date without asking — calling the guy and lying that Rachel is 'really sick' while Rachel is standing right there, perfectly healthy
jokes.explanation: Monica's controlling character fully realized — she's canceled a date Monica didn't authorize. The power being used against Rachel's interests (or is it for them?) is good character comedy. The lie is delivered with zero guilt.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I have to go. I dropped my socks in the dryer and I need to get them before they wrinkle.

jokes.text: Chandler emerges with a lame excuse: 'I dropped some socks.' Ross and Monica immediately see through it — Monica: 'You did not drop any socks!'
jokes.setup: Chandler has been lurking, obviously trying to kiss Monica in secret; he interrupts the moment with a flimsy excuse for being there
jokes.punchline: 'I dropped some socks' — an absurdly terrible cover story that fools no one, particularly Monica who calls it immediately
jokes.explanation: The specific terribleness of 'I dropped some socks' as an excuse is very funny — it's the kind of lie someone tells when they haven't thought for even a second. Chandler's bad lying is well-established, and 'You did not drop any socks!' being Monica's response (not 'why are you here') is good character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, you don't have a sock drawer. You have a sock pile. In the corner. With a chair on top of it.

jokes.text: Monica confronts Chandler about his lie and his kissing: 'What is the matter with you? Do you want to fall into the trap? I saw Dave, and he said you blew him off!'
jokes.setup: Monica discovers Chandler has been making excuses to come kiss her and has inadvertently sabotaged Rachel's date in the process
jokes.punchline: Monica's tirade reveals the absurd chain of consequences — Chandler's compulsive need to kiss Monica has now cost Rachel her date and Monica's carefully laid plans
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe moment — Chandler's inability to control himself is funny, and Monica's anger about the collateral damage is a good reveal. The underlying comedy is that their secret relationship is causing real-world chaos.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, I'm going to have to let you go from your decision-making position.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: As someone in a decision-making position, I've decided that's not happening.

jokes.text: Rachel fires Monica as her decision-maker. Monica: 'You can't fire me.' Rachel: 'I make your decisions, and I say I'm not fired! Ha!'
jokes.setup: Rachel decides to tell Ross she still loves him against Monica's advice; Monica refuses to accept being fired
jokes.punchline: Monica turns the logic against Rachel — 'I make your decisions, and I say I'm not fired' — using Rachel's own delegated authority to override her own firing
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever logical paradox — Monica using the delegated authority to block her own dismissal is a tidy, well-structured joke with real wit. The 'Ha!' at the end is the perfect Monica triumphant touch. This is the best payoff to the Monica-as-decision-maker arc. The logic is airtight and funny, and the structure is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'll help you with that door.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But first, you gotta kiss me.

jokes.text: You're fired. / You can't fire me. / I make your decisions, and I say I'm not fired! Ha!
jokes.setup: Rachel tries to end Monica's decision-making authority by firing her
jokes.punchline: Monica uses the very power being revoked to un-revoke it: 'I make your decisions, and I say I'm not fired!'
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever logical trap. Monica uses the authority being taken from her to prevent it from being taken — a perfect logical paradox played for comedy. 'I make your decisions, and I say I'm not fired! Ha!' is a great comedy construction: the logic is both airtight and completely insane. The 'Ha!' at the end is the cherry on top. High originality because the comedic premise is unusual and the execution is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You can't tell him! It'll ruin everything.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Look, relationships are like swing dancing. You have to have the right partner, the right timing, and you can't just throw yourself at someone mid-routine or you'll both end up on the floor.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Are we talking about swing dancing or...?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, some things are better left unsaid.

jokes.text: Monica, locked out: 'Come on, let me in!' Chandler: 'Having some trouble?' Monica: 'Rachel locked the door.' Chandler: 'I'll kick that door in if you give me some sugar.'
jokes.setup: Monica has been locked out by Rachel and is pleading to be let in; Chandler arrives and sees her predicament
jokes.punchline: Chandler uses Monica's vulnerability as leverage to extract a kiss ('some sugar') in exchange for kicking the door down — his compulsive kissing now has comedic bargaining power
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Chandler's compulsive need to kiss Monica gets turned into actual leverage. 'Give me some sugar' is a fun period expression. The joke ties together the locked-door situation and the secret relationship dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's like swing dancing. You have to let the guy lead, and if you're tense, it doesn't work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's true. I took a swing dancing class once, and my partner kept stepping on my feet because I was too stiff.

jokes.text: Monica tries to speak to Rachel in code in front of Ross: 'Remember that thing we just discussed that you wanted to do?' Rachel: 'What thing?' Monica: 'Rachel wants to take swing dance lessons. Which I think is a really stupid idea.'
jokes.setup: Monica is desperate to stop Rachel from telling Ross she loves him and tries to communicate this secretly in front of Ross
jokes.punchline: Her 'code' is transparently obvious — she invents 'swing dance lessons' as a stand-in for 'telling Ross you love him' and then argues against them ('it's dangerous, she won't get what she wants') in terms that clearly apply to the real situation
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed irony joke — the audience is ahead of Ross, who appears to take the swing dancing cover story at face value. Monica's argument against swing dancing ('dangerous, she won't get what she wants, who knows who she might hurt') maps perfectly onto the real situation. Good dramatic irony executed with commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I need to cancel an order. I sent five teddy bears to London, and I need them stopped before they arrive.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.line: Five teddy bears? Sir, that's not a massacre.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, to Emily it will be!

jokes.text: Ross, completely taking the swing dancing cover story at face value: 'Monica's right. Swing dancing can be tricky.'
jokes.setup: Monica has been transparently arguing against Rachel telling Ross she loves him using 'swing dancing' as a cover
jokes.punchline: Ross, entirely oblivious to the subtext, sincerely weighs in: 'Swing dancing can be tricky.' He means it literally
jokes.explanation: Ross's obliviousness is perfectly deployed. The deadpan 'swing dancing can be tricky' is funny because it's sincerely meant while being completely beside the point. It's also an inadvertent meta-commentary on his own relationship situation. High character integration — Ross's obliviousness to romantic subtext is a core character trait going back to the pilot.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We wanted to do something really special for you, Phoebe. We've been planning this trip for weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're taking you somewhere you've always wanted to go.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Somewhere exotic and amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: We're going to... Central Park!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Central Park? That's it? I walk through Central Park all the time. I once gave birth to triplets behind the Bethesda Terrace.

jokes.text: Ross: 'I have to use the phone. I got to cancel those five, giant teddy bears I sent to Emily.' Monica: 'My God! Think of the massacre.'
jokes.setup: Following the mulched roses, Ross has apparently also sent five giant teddy bears to Emily
jokes.punchline: Monica's dark reaction — 'Think of the massacre' — treats the potential destruction of the teddy bears with mock horror, applying the same dark logic as the rose-mulching
jokes.explanation: A dark topper on the established joke about Emily's destructive response to Ross's romantic gestures. 'Think of the massacre' applied to teddy bears is genuinely funny — it escalates the dark humor of the situation. The escalation from 72 roses to five giant teddy bears also reveals how over-the-top Ross's gestures are.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't believe we're not actually going to Central Park. I was really looking forward to it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And what if we run into a street performer? They always want to give me a high-five, and my hands are very sensitive.

jokes.text: The friends reveal the 'trip' they've planned for Phoebe to make up for missing London: a picnic in Central Park
jokes.setup: Everyone feels guilty that Phoebe missed London; they've planned a 'little trip together' to compensate
jokes.punchline: The 'trip' is revealed to be a picnic in Central Park — right near her house. The anticlimax is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection/anticlimax — the buildup ('we decided to take a little trip together!') followed by 'Central Park' is a reliable structure. Phoebe's indignant response ('That sucks! I just came from there!') sells it. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, could you BE any more of a lip-locking machine right now?

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'That's not a trip! I just came from there. What'll we high-five about at the stupid park?'
jokes.setup: The friends have revealed their 'trip' for Phoebe is a picnic in Central Park
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's specific objection — 'What'll we high-five about at the stupid park?' — reveals that for her, a trip's value is measured in its excitement-generating high-five moments
jokes.explanation: The specific detail of 'What'll we high-five about?' is a great character moment — Phoebe's enthusiasm for life measured in high-five-worthy events is delightfully specific. The addition of 'stupid park' shows she's genuinely offended by the inadequacy of the gesture.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's a cultural thing! In some countries, men greet each other with a kiss on the lips.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, in THIS country, we call that sexual assault!

jokes.text: Chandler, indignant about the Central Park idea: 'It's right by my house. All right! I'm going home to bask in the triumph of my Central Park idea.'
jokes.setup: Everyone agrees the Central Park picnic idea is terrible; it's clearly Chandler's idea
jokes.punchline: Chandler, completely ignoring that his idea has just been roundly rejected, announces he's going home to 'bask in the triumph of my Central Park idea' — an absurdly deluded response to failure
jokes.explanation: Chandler's self-satisfied delusion about a clearly failed idea is good character comedy. 'Bask in the triumph' applied to something everyone just called stupid is a funny ironic contrast. The 'it's right by my house' as his only defense is also good.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Who came up with the Atlantic City plan?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I did!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, I did!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, I mentioned it first.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But I organized the logistics.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I drove us there though!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So basically, nobody knows.

jokes.text: Joey confronts Chandler about the kissing: 'I need to say it makes me very uncomfortable...just stop it! Just bringing some culture to the group.' Joey: 'That's fine. Just don't bring it in my mouth. It makes me want to puke.'
jokes.setup: Joey has figured out Chandler keeps kissing people as a 'European goodbye' and finds it deeply uncomfortable
jokes.punchline: Joey's line 'Just don't bring it in my mouth. It makes me want to puke' is a viscerally funny, blunt statement of homophobic discomfort (filtered through Joey's oblivious directness) that completely ignores the cover story
jokes.explanation: Joey's blunt 'don't bring it in my mouth, it makes me want to puke' is a great character-specific line — his directness and lack of filter make this funnier than a more polished objection would be. The rewatch bonus is in knowing Chandler is actually kissing Monica and Joey has no idea.

jokes.text: Just bringing some culture to the group. / That's fine. Just don't bring it in my mouth. It makes me want to puke.
jokes.setup: Joey defends his kissing habit as cultural enrichment.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'just don't bring it in my mouth' is an inadvertently strange (and graphic) way of objecting to a kiss; followed immediately by the blunt 'It makes me want to puke.'
jokes.explanation: 'Don't bring it in my mouth' is a funny line because it's both literally accurate and strangely phrased. The escalation to 'makes me want to puke' — delivered with Chandler's signature flat affect — is sharp. Good comic economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I'm reading about the latest paleontological discoveries in the Mesozoic Era, the geopolitical implications of trade tariffs, and a rather compelling exposé on municipal infrastructure.

jokes.text: The Atlantic City plan is announced to Phoebe, and everyone immediately fights over whose idea it was
jokes.setup: Phoebe is told they're going to Atlantic City for the weekend instead of Central Park
jokes.punchline: Everyone simultaneously claims credit: 'Mine!' / 'Wait, it was my plan' / 'No...I said we needed a new plan. And I came up with Atlantic City, which is the new plan.'
jokes.explanation: Generic group comedy — everyone taking credit for a good idea is a reliable if well-worn sitcom beat. Chandler's specific claim ('I said we needed a new plan, and I came up with Atlantic City, which is the new plan') has some logical absurdity to it. Functional but unremarkable.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, I'm right about this. People are wrong all the time and they don't even realize it. Like, did you know that the human body is 60% water? No wait, it's 70%. Actually, I think it might be 65%... I mean, the point is, people confidently state facts they're not even sure about, which is exactly what I'm talking about!

jokes.text: We thought that this afternoon we'd all go away for the whole weekend to Atlantic City!
jokes.setup: The Central Park idea flopped; they've replaced it with a proper trip to make Phoebe feel special
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'Central Park' to 'Atlantic City' mirrors the first joke's structure but reverses the anti-climax — this time the reveal is genuinely exciting
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands partly because Central Park set up such low expectations. Structural callback to the earlier joke. Straightforward setup for the Atlantic City runner.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? What do you mean 'I know'? I just told you I'm in love with you! I can't believe you're being so cruel right now.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I'm going to go pack. I'm going to go pack my ass off.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is excited about Atlantic City; Chandler announces he's going to pack
jokes.punchline: He adds 'my ass off' — an intensifier that is both characteristically Chandler (mild profanity for mild enthusiasm) and slightly funny in its proportion
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh, mostly on delivery. 'Pack my ass off' is a mild bit of Chandler enthusiasm that plays better in the room than on paper. Not particularly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know, I know, it's ridiculous. I'm being ridiculous. I'm laughing at myself because... because what else am I supposed to do? I mean, this is insane. It's completely insane. I'm insane. Do you hear how insane I sound right now? Because I sound insane. Very, very insane.

jokes.text: I'm going to go pack. I'm going to go pack my ass off.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is excited about Atlantic City
jokes.punchline: 'Pack my ass off' — the unexpected intensity of her packing enthusiasm expressed through mild profanity
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's occasional casual profanity for maximum enthusiasm is a reliable laugh. 'Pack my ass off' is funnier than expected from her. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I was floating above myself, looking down, and I was like, 'Wow, she really should have said something to Ross years ago.'

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And then floating me was just shaking her head at regular me like, 'Girl, that outfit does NOT work with those shoes.'

jokes.text: Ross reads the newspaper when Rachel approaches him to confess; she asks 'What's it about?' and he says, deadpan: 'The events from around the globe.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is working up the courage to tell Ross something important; she nervously tries small talk by asking about his newspaper
jokes.punchline: Ross's completely literal, grandly pompous answer — 'The events from around the globe' — describes a newspaper the way no human ever would
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical. Ross's pedantry and pomposity captured in six words: 'The events from around the globe.' It describes a newspaper in the most self-importantly literal way possible. High character integration — this is exactly how Ross would answer. Genuinely funny and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So let me get this straight. My wife is missing, and I have no idea where she is. I mean, what kind of husband doesn't know where his wife is?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: "Oh, where's Rachel?" "I don't know, she could be anywhere! Peru? The grocery store? Who knows!"

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm a paleontologist! I can identify a fossilized bone from three million years ago, but I can't tell you if my wife is in the apartment!

jokes.text: Rachel's nervous rambling before her confession: 'Once at work, I thought carbon dating is fossilized...' — trails off mid-sentence realizing it's irrelevant
jokes.setup: Rachel is building up to telling Ross she loves him; she keeps stalling and says 'People can be wrong. Once at work, I thought carbon dating is fossilized—'
jokes.punchline: She starts an anecdote about carbon dating — clearly something Ross-adjacent that she's heard him discuss — before catching herself: 'I'm really trying to tell you something here.'
jokes.explanation: Rachel's stalling with Ross-specific jargon (carbon dating) is a nice character-specific touch — she's so nervous she's reaching for things Ross talks about. The abandoned sentence is funny in its irrelevance. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know! See? I told you! I was right!

jokes.text: Rachel: 'What? Was that a joke? Because it's mean.' Ross: 'I'm so dead serious! I'm totally serious! Why are you laughing?'
jokes.setup: Ross has responded to Rachel's love confession with 'I'm not sure what to do with that right now' — Rachel initially thinks he's joking
jokes.punchline: Ross is baffled that she's laughing because he's completely serious — his literal-mindedness making him unable to see why the phrasing is absurd
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous joke — Ross's total inability to see why his response was funny is itself funny. 'I'm so dead serious!' only makes it funnier. This beat extends the previous joke's impact nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're going to Atlantic City!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah! We're gonna roll some bones, baby!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Did you just say 'roll some bones'?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? It's a thing!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, it's not a thing. You just made it a thing, and now it's awkward.

jokes.text: Rachel explains why she's laughing: 'I heard it! And it's ridiculous! I mean, you're married! You're married, and it's just ridiculous! When I said it, I sort of floated up out of my body...'
jokes.setup: Ross doesn't understand why Rachel is laughing after confessing her love
jokes.punchline: Rachel's self-aware explanation — she 'floated up out of her body' and then heard herself say it and thought 'you are such an idiot' — is a funny piece of self-aware absurdism
jokes.explanation: Rachel's out-of-body experience framing for her own stupid decision is a good self-aware beat. The 'floating Rachel' was like 'you are such an idiot' is a funny way to externalize self-criticism. Good emotional honesty turned into comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Who's sitting in front?

jokes.text: Ross: 'Well, I am married.' Rachel: 'I know.' Ross: 'Though I haven't spoken to her since the wedding.'
jokes.setup: Ross is explaining why he can't act on Rachel's declaration — he's married to Emily
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts his own defense by noting that he 'hasn't spoken to her since the wedding' — revealing that his marriage is functionally already in complete collapse
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic understatement — Ross invokes his marriage as the reason he can't respond to Rachel, then immediately reveals the marriage is already a fiction in practice. 'Though I haven't spoken to her since the wedding' said as a mild afterthought is very funny dark comedy. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Phoebe's in labor!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We need to get her to the hospital!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This is it! This is the big moment!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Everyone stay calm. I'll call an ambulance.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'm ready. Let's do this!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You got this, Phoebe!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: High five! This is amazing!

jokes.text: Rachel: 'I'm sorry. That's not funny.' Ross: 'Actually, it kind of is.'
jokes.setup: Ross has just noted he hasn't spoken to Emily since the wedding; Rachel offers condolences
jokes.punchline: Ross himself acknowledges the comedy of his terrible situation: 'Actually, it kind of is.' His self-awareness about the absurdity of his life is the joke
jokes.explanation: Four words — 'Actually, it kind of is' — do a lot of work. Ross's self-awareness about the comedy of his situation is a rare moment of his own self-deprecation, and it bonds him and Rachel in a funny-sad moment. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I'm just saying goodbye to my friends.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, while you're at it, why don't you just do that thing we talked about in the bathroom?

jokes.text: Ross riffing on his situation, escalating: 'My wife won't return my calls. / I don't know where my wife is. / "Hey, Ross! Where's the missus?" "Don't know!"'
jokes.setup: Having acknowledged that his situation is funny, Ross leans into it, listing the comedic indignities of his marriage collapsing
jokes.punchline: He escalates through increasingly bleak facts about his marriage — culminating in the imagined social exchange 'Hey, Ross! Where's the missus?' / 'Don't know!' — which captures the absurd humiliation of his situation perfectly
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure here is excellent — each beat is funnier than the last. 'My wife won't return my calls' → 'I don't know where my wife is' → the imagined social humiliation of 'Where's the missus?' / 'Don't know!' The last beat is the best: the forced cheerful voice of the imagined interlocutor against Ross's flat 'Don't know!' is perfectly constructed. This is good joke-writing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, you realize that most people don't actually have sex in public places, right?

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Oh God. Things won't be weird between us, right? Was that stupid — me telling you that?' Ross: 'I'm glad you did. If nothing else...it's always great when someone tells you they love you.' Rachel: 'That's what I said!'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to comfort Rachel after her confession; he says 'it's always great when someone tells you they love you'
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately recognizes this as the exact thing she said to Monica earlier to defend her plan — 'That's what I said!' — validating her earlier point and completing the circle
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural callback — Ross's comfort echoes Rachel's own earlier argument, vindicating her decision. 'That's what I said!' is a good button. It rewards attentive viewers and gives Rachel a small victory in the moment.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Let's roll some bones. Hey, Joey! High-five for rolling bones!' [High-fives himself]
jokes.setup: Everyone is excitedly heading to Atlantic City
jokes.punchline: Joey calls out to himself and then high-fives himself for his enthusiasm about gambling — talking to himself in third person and generating his own hype
jokes.explanation: Joey talking to himself in third person and self-high-fiving is a great character moment. The specific phrase 'Let's roll some bones' with its enthusiastic casino energy followed by the self-high-five is physically funny. High character integration.

jokes.text: Joey, noticing Phoebe: 'Pheebs, you're leaking.' Everyone: 'Oh my God! Your water broke!'
jokes.setup: Everyone is excitedly heading to Atlantic City; Phoebe's water breaks
jokes.punchline: Joey's clinical-yet-casual description of Phoebe's water breaking — 'Pheebs, you're leaking' — is a hilariously understated way to announce a major event
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Pheebs, you're leaking' is an extraordinary piece of deadpan understatement — Joey reduces a dramatic medical event to the vocabulary he might use to describe a leaking faucet. The economy is nearly perfect (three words), the character integration is excellent (only Joey would phrase it this way), and it's immediately quotable. The contrast between Joey's casual observation and everyone else's panic is perfectly structured.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Well, don't worry. I call shotgun.' [after Phoebe's water breaks and they need to rush to the hospital]
jokes.setup: Phoebe's water has broken; they need to get her to the hospital immediately
jokes.punchline: Joey's first instinct in a medical emergency is to call shotgun — his priorities completely unmoved by the urgency of the situation
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey — his response to a medical emergency is completely self-interested but not malicious. 'I call shotgun' said with zero panic while everyone else is freaking out is a perfect character beat. The economy is excellent; the juxtaposition with the seriousness of the moment amplifies the comedy. Very quotable. Only slightly below 'Pheebs, you're leaking' in impact because that one is more unexpected.

jokes.text: Monica, in the chaos, high-fives Phoebe: 'Honey! High-five! The babies are coming!'
jokes.setup: Everyone is rushing Phoebe to the hospital in a panic
jokes.punchline: Monica stops to give Phoebe a high-five in the middle of the medical emergency, calling back to Phoebe's earlier complaint about wanting something to high-five about
jokes.explanation: A callback that actually earns its laugh — Phoebe complained about not having a high-five-worthy moment, and now she gets one (albeit at the cost of her water breaking). Monica stopping mid-emergency to high-five Phoebe honors Phoebe's earlier complaint while being completely absurd. The structure is tight and the callback is genuinely satisfying.

jokes.text: Phoebe, mid-labor emergency: 'Remember when my water broke?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe's water has just broken; everyone is scrambling
jokes.punchline: Phoebe refers to it in the past tense — 'Remember when my water broke?' — as if it's already a cherished memory, with zero urgency, as though it happened years ago instead of seconds ago
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Phoebe line. The immediate nostalgia — referring to something that happened eight seconds ago as 'remember when' — is perfectly absurdist and perfectly in character. Phoebe's detachment from urgency and her tendency to speak about ordinary things with wistful retrospect is captured perfectly. High economy, great character integration, very quotable.

jokes.text: Chandler, in confessional/aside: 'I had to kiss Phoebe and Rachel every time I left the room.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has been going around kissing people to maintain the cover story that it's his 'European goodbye'
jokes.punchline: He reveals that the cover story has spiraled out of control — he's now had to kiss multiple women including Phoebe and Rachel to maintain the lie
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the European goodbye running gag — Chandler reveals the full comedic consequence of his cover story. The image of him having to kiss Phoebe and Rachel to maintain a lie he told to cover for kissing Monica is a good escalation. The confessional format works well here.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'It's too bad they didn't see us having sex.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just said he had to kiss Phoebe and Rachel because they saw him kiss Monica and he used it as a cover
jokes.punchline: He extends the logic to its darkest possible conclusion — if kissing required kissing everyone, then if they'd been caught having sex... The implication is left to the audience
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp joke that earns its dark edge. The logical extension of 'if they saw us kiss, I had to kiss everyone' → 'too bad they didn't see us having sex' is both funny and slightly shocking. It's completely Chandler — the kind of joke only he would make about his own situation. The economy is excellent (nine words), the structure is perfect (follows logically from the previous line), and it's genuinely quotable. This is the best tag joke in the episode.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Do you know anything about women?'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just said 'it's too bad they didn't see us having sex'
jokes.punchline: Monica's flat 'Do you know anything about women?' as a button — the perfect exasperated straight-woman tag to Chandler's joke
jokes.explanation: A clean button on the episode's final joke. Monica's exasperation is delivered with perfect economy and timing. It's not an exceptional joke on its own but it's the right close for the episode — Chandler's obliviousness met with Monica's weary practicality.

jokes.text: It's too bad they didn't see us having sex. / Do you know anything about women?
jokes.setup: Monica suggests Chandler could have let them see them having sex as an equivalent disclosure
jokes.punchline: Chandler's withering 'Do you know anything about women?' — the irony that Monica, a woman, apparently doesn't know anything about women
jokes.explanation: Superb button on the episode. The joke is structurally perfect: Chandler asks Monica if she knows anything about women — she IS a woman — and the implication is that her suggestion was so wrong it disqualifies her from the category. The economy is excellent, the irony is delicious, and it's the ideal closing beat. This is the kind of joke that gets a big finish-of-episode laugh.

tmdb_overview: Ross continues to try and mend his marriage to Emily. When Chandler accidentally kisses Monica in front of everyone before leaving for work, he tries to recover by kissing Rachel and Phoebe as well. Meanwhile, Phoebe starts getting irritated by everyone's London stories.
insight: Character comedy dominates 54 jokes, but 74.2 score signals inconsistent landing.
